overview: Ovimbundu names communities of Angola’s central highlands, not one kingdom. Earlier political loyalties centered on places such as Bailundo, Bié and Huambo. A broader shared identity developed through commerce, colonial pressures and missionary institutions. This map’s 1878 to 1914 block compresses that varied history.

periods.title: Several highland polities
periods.summary: Caravan commerce connected distinct kingdoms rather than a single Ovimbundu state.

periods.title: Colonial rule and changing livelihoods
periods.summary: Political subordination accompanied new opportunities and pressures in farming and trade.

items.text: Bié was a major inland trading hub with routes toward both Luanda and Benguela. Visiting traders established households with women, children, helpers and enslaved people. The caravan network moved through settled communities; it was not simply a line of travelers crossing empty land.

After the loss of political autonomy, farming did not simply stop prospering. Neto traces increased maize and bean production and local commerce, helped by the railway after 1910. Some households adapted successfully even while colonial authorities reduced the power of local rulers.

That adaptation came under unequal conditions. Missionaries reported taxes and forced labor imposed on peasants; later European settlement, labor demands and pressure on land deepened hardship. Economic growth in one decade should not hide who carried its burdens.

During his 1929 to 1930 fieldwork, Hambly described families helping build houses: men assembled walls while women and children supplied wet clay. Children enjoyed trampling it with their feet. Building day could include an excellent excuse for getting muddy.

Hambly also saw pits containing maize husks and sweet-potato refuse, and reported use of the bush for toileting. These are specific early twentieth-century observations, not evidence that all highland villages shared one sanitation system.

Hambly’s accounts from his 1929 to 1930 fieldwork include spinning tops, counting games and children pretending to lead caravans. Boys lashed small loads between forked sticks and marched singing. Even make-believe travelers knew that properly packed luggage mattered.

sections.title: Objects in ordinary and spiritual life

items.text: The Museu Nacional catalogue records wooden spoons, a flour sieve, baskets and a comb in Celenia Pires’s collection, donated in 1936. Such objects turn attention from kings to cooking, carrying, sorting food and personal care: indispensable skills that rarely headline political histories.

A small perforated gourd rattle collected at Dondi accompanied a diviner’s songs, according to notes dated 1932. Its seeds made the sound. The object helps document the music surrounding spiritual consultation, without establishing that the divination worked.

A carved woman collected at Benguela shows a married woman’s hairstyle and fibre plaits described as a fertility charm. Museum curators suggest possible use by a diviner. The wood, cloth and metal embody careful craft; the precise use remains uncertain.

At Dondi, the Currie Institute opened for boys in 1914; the Means School followed for girls in 1916. Mission stations sent selected pupils onward. Girls gained educational opportunities, but training also reflected restrictive expectations about their future family roles.

“Viovusenge” means “things of the bush.” It is the Umbundu title of Mabel Stokey’s book printed at Camundongo in 1916. This attested Latin-letter sample comes just after the map interval; its Portuguese title translation appears in the same volume.

A 1926 schoolbook on tropical hygiene was printed in Portuguese and Umbundu. Madaleno Chipa translated its Umbundu text. Health education therefore involved local language expertise and printing work, alongside the mission’s religious project.

ending.text: Portuguese domination curtailed the autonomy of highland polities, but the Ovimbundu did not disappear in 1914. Farming, trade and community life continued through colonial restructuring. The end of this imported map block is not the end of a people.
